sections.overview: The common cockchafer is a large European scarab beetle whose adults fly on spring evenings and whose white grubs live underground for about three years. Its mass flights, once classic in parts of Switzerland, have largely faded in recent decades.
sections.identification: Adults are 25–30 mm long, the largest native cockchafer in Switzerland, with a dark head, a shiny black pronotum covered in short hairs and a long, flat pygidium at the tip of the abdomen. Males have longer antennae with a large fan-like club. The grub is dull white, up to about 40–46 mm, with a black abdominal tip and strong jaws, and rests curled in an arc. The consulted species references do not provide a reliable adult body mass for identification; no weight is estimated here.
sections.habitat: It occurs in temperate Europe, in meadows, farmland, forest edges and suburbs, and prefers soft soil with a medium cover of vegetation for egg laying. Adults fly towards forest edges, groves and trees on rounded hilltops or ridges, guided by the silhouette of the trees.
sections.diet: Adults eat the leaves of deciduous trees, especially oaks, and also beech and larch, mostly in May. The grubs eat roots, including those of grasses, cereals and many other plants, in meadows and cultivated soil.
sections.behavior: Adults are nocturnal and active at dusk, flying from about mid-April for around two weeks in some Swiss valleys and on mild evenings in May, and they are attracted to lights. Grubs stay buried until pupation; on a flat surface they try to move sideways, curled up.
sections.reproduction: Females lay about 20 eggs at a time in soft soil. Grubs hatch a few weeks later and develop underground. The cycle normally lasts three years, ending in the big flights, but it can last four years in mountain regions and has occasionally shortened to two with warming. Since 2003 it no longer always follows the three-year rhythm in Valais.
sections.ecology: Heavy leaf-eating in May leaves oaks and larches stripped, but defoliated trees regrow replacement shoots from June and are green again in summer, with possibly some loss of growth. Grubs can damage meadows, lawns and crops. Fungi of the genus Beauveria are used against them in crops, and it is neither useful nor allowed to treat forests.
sections.conservation: Animal Diversity Web lists the species with no special status, but no recent global assessment was read. In Switzerland the once-classic mass flights around Basel, Bern and central Switzerland have largely disappeared or are no longer distinct, so local abundance has changed greatly.
